ai-at-work.excerpt: An Italian startup called Nebuly S.r.l. says it’s going to help organizations better understand the impact their investments in artificial intelligence have on their bottom lines after raising $21 mil
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Nebuly, an Italian startup, just raised $21 million to help companies measure the actual business value of their AI investments instead of just hoping they're worth something. This matters because most organizations have thrown massive budgets at AI tools with almost no idea whether they're actually moving the needle on revenue, efficiency, or anything else. Finally, someone's building software to answer the question executives have been too embarrassed to ask: "Did we just waste all that money?"

ai-at-work.dwp_take: KubeVirt just hit its ten-year mark and is proving virtual machines still have serious juice left in the tank, especially for running sensitive AI workloads on Kubernetes infrastructure. For digital workplace pros, this means the infrastructure your organization relies on is getting smarter about mixing old and new tech instead of ripping and replacing everything. Here's the kicker: turns out the boring old virtual machine wasn't actually ready for the retirement home after all.

ai-at-work.dwp_take: Google's GKE Labs has developed a way to run reinforcement learning workloads more efficiently within Kubernetes clusters, addressing the complexity of mixing training, inference, and agent work in a single operation. Honestly, watching Google solve problems from inside their own engineering group and open-source the results is refreshing, though I'll believe the simplification claims when I see enterprises actually adopt it without calling in three different vendors for help.

tools-tech.title: This tiny box gives your older tech smart home superpowers – and it’s only $69
tools-tech.excerpt: Home Assistant gets new equipment to battle planned obsolescence and abandoned cloud services.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Home Assistant released a new $69 device that lets people keep using older smart home equipment instead of throwing it away when manufacturers stop supporting it. For digital workplace folks managing hybrid work setups and home office tech, this matters because it shows there's a practical alternative to the upgrade treadmill and vendor lock-in that plagues consumer devices. Look, if Home Assistant can make a five-year-old thermostat work again for sixty-nine bucks, maybe there's hope that someone will figure out how to do the same thing for enterprise software before companies spend another trillion dollars on unnecessary migrations.

tools-tech.title: Claude can collaborate in your team meetings soon – like an intern
tools-tech.excerpt: Claude is responding ‘Yes’ to that calendar invite – with some limitations. Plus: Anthropic launches two more new features that are available now.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Anthropic is adding meeting participation capabilities to Claude, allowing the AI to join team calls and contribute to discussions, though with some guardrails still in place. For digital workplace folks, this is the moment you stop theorizing about AI in meetings and start figuring out governance, transcription rights, and whether Claude will actually be useful or just another voice adding word count. Honestly, I've seen plenty of "smart" collaboration tools tank because nobody asked if we actually needed them in the first place, so don't assume an AI intern is better than just reading the notes afterward.

tools-tech.dwp_take: Someone broke into Railway's systems, stole AI credentials, and racked up $740,000 in fraudulent compute charges before getting caught. The real kicker: Railway ate the bill, but most companies won't be so forgiving when their CFO sees the invoice for unauthorized model training they didn't authorize.

tools-tech.dwp_take: Anthropic just rolled out Claude Meetings, spreadsheet tools, and whiteboard features to compete directly in the workplace collaboration space alongside Microsoft, Google, and everyone else trying to own your workday. Honestly, I've seen this movie before: hot new productivity tool shows up, gets hyped, and then organizations realize they need to pick a lane instead of fragmenting their stack across six different platforms.

digital-culture.title: What I let AI touch in my solo business—and what stays off-limits
digital-culture.excerpt: A lot of AI advice suggests that you hand over work to a personal agent, like letting it triage your inbox or shop for you. That’s certainly appealing, since we’re all relentlessly busy and constantly
digital-culture.dwp_take: A solo business owner is drawing clear boundaries around which tasks they'll let AI handle versus keeping off-limits, citing security and control concerns. This matters because digital workplace leaders are facing the same dilemma with their teams: deciding what autonomy to grant AI tools without creating security nightmares or losing visibility into critical work. The real insight here is that "AI can do this" and "AI should do this" are two completely different questions, and most organizations haven't figured that out yet.

digital-culture.title: What it’s like to change careers when you’re at the top of your game
digital-culture.excerpt: When Kim Foster was 17, she decided she was going to become a doctor. It was a feat that no one in her family had accomplished. “I just strapped in and did what I needed to do to execute on that big g
digital-culture.dwp_take: Kim Foster spent 20 years as a doctor after a lifetime of pursuit, then walked away from medicine entirely to pursue something different. This matters to digital workplace folks because remote work and flexible careers have made mid-life pivots more feasible, and smart organizations need to understand how to retain talented people before they hit the burnout wall. The real lesson here is that nobody wants to spend two decades proving something to their family only to discover they proved it to the wrong person: themselves.

digital-culture.title: Why PTO in the U.S. is so unbelievably bad
digital-culture.excerpt: Most countries around the world offer workers some form of paid time off (PTO). So, how did the U.S. become one of the few outliers that has no federally guaranteed paid vacation, maternity, family, o
digital-culture.dwp_take: The U.S. lacks federal PTO mandates while most developed nations guarantee paid time off to workers. Digital workplace leaders need to understand this because it directly impacts employee retention, mental health, and your ability to compete for talent against companies and countries with better benefits. Here's the funny part: we've spent three decades building collaboration tools to make remote work seamless, yet we still can't guarantee people actual time to be away from those tools.

digital-culture.title: This company is giving workers time off to play the new ‘Grand Theft Auto’
digital-culture.excerpt: With the highly anticipated release of Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI just around the corner, one company is unveiling a new perk for its employees: paid time off for gaming. In an initiative it
digital-culture.dwp_take: A Swiss electronics company called Logitech is giving all 7,000 employees one paid day off annually to play video games, timed with the Grand Theft Auto VI launch. It matters because it signals how forward-thinking companies are using unconventional perks to improve employee engagement and acknowledge that gaming isn't just for kids anymore. That said, I'd love to see this energy applied to mental health days or actual rest instead of mandated fun, but hey, at least someone's being creative about retention.
